title: Katakana N-Row — ナ ニ ヌ ネ ノ

points.name: ナ
points.explanation: ナ makes the same 'na' sound as hiragana な. Visually, ナ looks remarkably like a capital Roman 'T' rotated slightly, or more precisely: a horizontal stroke crossed by a diagonal going down to the lower right. It has two strokes and resembles a simplified 'na' made with just the essential lines. Compare this to the more complex hiragana な, which has four strokes and a loop. ナ appears in ナイフ (knife), ナース (nurse), and ナイト (night / knight). The katakana system's angular simplicity makes many characters like ナ feel very printable and clear.
rules: ナ has two strokes: a horizontal and a diagonal going lower-right.
Memory: ナ looks like a cross or a '+' sign with the left arm removed.

points.name: ニ
points.explanation: ニ makes the same 'ni' sound as hiragana に. Visually, ニ is disarmingly simple — just two horizontal strokes, one shorter above and one longer below, like a Roman numeral II but with different lengths, or a simplified version of the Chinese character 二 (two). In fact, this is not a coincidence: katakana ニ was derived from part of a kanji character. ニ appears in ニュース (news), ニット (knit), and ニーズ (needs — as in 'market needs'). The double-horizontal shape makes ニ one of the easiest katakana to write.
rules: ニ = two horizontal strokes. Possibly the simplest katakana character to write.
ニュース (news) uses ニュ — ニ + small ュ = 'nyu'. You'll see ニュース everywhere.
points.flashcardAnswer: ni — same sound as に; looks like two horizontal strokes

points.name: ヌ
points.explanation: ヌ makes the same 'nu' sound as hiragana ぬ. Visually, ヌ has two strokes: a diagonal cross and a sweeping curve at the bottom — it looks somewhat like the Roman letter 'X' but with the lower diagonal replaced by a curve that sweeps right. Compare this to the very complex hiragana ぬ — ヌ is a dramatic simplification. ヌ is one of the less common katakana characters since the 'nu' sound is relatively rare in English loanwords. The most notable example is ヌードル (noodle), though ヌードル itself is less common than just using the Japanese word うどん or ラーメン.
rules: Same 'nu' as ぬ — 'n' + flat, unrounded Japanese 'u'.
ヌ resembles an 'X' where the lower-right stroke curves around instead of continuing diagonally.
ヌ is relatively rare in everyday loanwords — but worth knowing for completeness.

examples.english: menu (note: ヌ in ニュ pattern)

points.name: ネ
points.explanation: ネ makes the same 'ne' sound as hiragana ね. Visually, ネ looks like a cross or plus-sign with a diagonal stroke extending to the lower right — some learners describe it as a 'net' post or a stick figure with a diagonal arm. The character has three main strokes and creates a recognizable shape. Compare to hiragana ね, which has a complex looping structure. ネ appears in ネクタイ (necktie), ネット (internet / net), and ネイル (nail / nail art). ネイル is particularly useful since nail art is a huge industry in Japan.
rules: ネ has the shape of a cross with a diagonal stroke — three strokes total.
ネット (net/internet) and ネクタイ (necktie) are among the most useful ネ words.
points.flashcardAnswer: ne — same sound as ね; looks like a cross with a diagonal stroke

points.name: ノ
points.explanation: ノ makes the same 'no' sound as hiragana の. Visually, ノ is the simplest possible katakana character — just a single diagonal stroke going from upper-left to lower-right. It looks like a slash '/' or a katakana version of the Roman letter 'N' reduced to its most essential diagonal. Compare this to hiragana の, which is a complete loop. ノ appears in ノート (notebook), ノック (knock), and ノイズ (noise). ノート (notebook) is particularly essential for students — it's one of the first words you'd look up as a student in Japan.
rules: ノ = one single diagonal stroke. The simplest katakana character to write.
ノート (notebook) is essential student vocabulary — もしノートを貸してください is 'Please lend me your notebook'.
points.flashcardAnswer: no — same sound as の; just one diagonal stroke (the simplest katakana!)

chapterPractice.prompt: What sound does this katakana make?
chapterPractice.explanation: ニ makes the 'ni' sound — same as hiragana に. It's just two horizontal strokes, making it one of the easiest katakana characters to both read and write.

chapterPractice.prompt: Which katakana character is a single diagonal stroke?
chapterPractice.explanation: ノ (no) is just one diagonal stroke — making it the simplest katakana character. It looks like a slash '/' and sounds like the 'no' in 'note'.

chapterPractice.prompt: What does this katakana word mean?
chapterPractice.explanation: ノート (nooto) means 'notebook'. ノ (no) + ー (long o) + ト (to) = nooto. This is essential school vocabulary in Japan — students use ノート constantly for class notes.

chapterPractice.prompt: What does this katakana word mean?
chapterPractice.explanation: ニュース (nyuusu) means 'news'. ニュ (nyu, a combination) + ー (long u) + ス (su) = nyuusu. You'll encounter ニュース constantly — on TV, on apps, in conversation.
